title: Verifying generated content and checking sources

opening.headline: Before using the plausible figures and quotations provided by AI, we will organize what and how to check.
body: I asked AI to draft the report, and it clearly contained market size and growth figures. I put it into the report without confirmation, but at the meeting a question was asked about the source, and when I looked up the source, the figure was nowhere to be found. Just because AI seems confident in its answer doesn't mean it's right.

In this class, we will first look at why AI can confidently say something is wrong. Next, learn the flow of distinguishing between figures, citations, and laws, which are items that require verification of sources, and comparing claims with the original document. Lastly, in cases where verification procedures are applied to externally presented materials, determine for yourself whether the procedures are sufficient.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain situations where product verification is necessary
You can distinguish between items that require verification of sources (figures, quotations, laws)
You can determine whether the verification process is sufficient

screens.title: A plausible number was put in, but it turned out to be wrong.
screens.lead: Read the scene below and think at what stage you should have checked.

visual.alt: A scene where figures from a draft report written by AI are questioned at a meeting about the source.
labels: Where do these numbers come from?

paragraphs: I asked AI to draft the report. The draft that came back had clear market size and growth figures, and the sentences were natural. Because I was busy, I didn't check it and just put it into the report.
A few days later, at a meeting, someone asked where this number came from. When I looked for the source, I couldn't find that figure anywhere. AI created a plausible value.

This doesn't happen because AI tries to be wrong. Because the model answers based on patterns in the data it learned, it can create answers that seem correct. This class is a time to understand that and organize what and how to check.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Are the numbers looking accurate and the numbers being accurate the same? After class, you will be able to answer this question with evidence.

screens.outro: Let me first think about whether you have had a similar experience.

screens.title: If you have ever written without confirmation
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: What were the risks if you wrote the results without checking them?
items.answer: If unchecked content is incorrect, the responsibility goes to the person who wrote it. This may reduce the reliability of the report or lead to incorrect judgments. The risk lies not only in being wrong, but in going out there being wrong.

items.prompt: Have you ever had a date or definition wrong?
items.answer: Incorrect definitions, dates, and facts are typical errors. Even one mistake can shake the trust of the entire article. The shorter the fact, the less noticeable it is and the easier it is to overlook it.

items.prompt: Were there non-existent papers or citations? Didn't you say things definitively that were unclear?
items.answer: Inventing citations, research, and sources where none exist, as well as giving overconfident answers to vague questions, are also common errors. Neither can be distinguished by wording alone, so you'll need to check the source directly.

screens.outro: Let’s first check the principle of why this error occurs.

screens.title: Why Verification is Necessary: Confident Errors
screens.lead: The following flashcards illustrate four ways AI can be wrong. When you select a card, it flips over. Select the right arrow to go to the next card.

visual.alt: An icon indicating the type of error is placed on the front of each card.

cards.back: This is a phenomenon in which a model presents information that is not true as if it were plausible. OpenAI explains that ChatGPT answers based on patterns in the data it has learned, so it may produce incorrect or misleading output. Typical examples are incorrect definitions, dates, and facts.

This is an error that creates citations, studies, papers, or references that do not actually exist. Even if the title and author are plausible, they may not exist. For citations, you must find the original text to check if it actually exists.
The model can speak confidently even if the answer is wrong. Speaking with confidence is not evidence of accuracy. Giving overconfident answers to vague or complex questions is of the same type.

The model was trained with data up to a certain point in time, and subsequent events cannot be reflected unless tools such as search are used. Tools like search, code interpreters, data analytics, and deep research can improve accuracy, but we recommend checking important information from trusted sources.

screens.outro: Now that you know the types of errors, let's distinguish which items absolutely require source verification.

screens.title: Items that require verification of sources: figures, quotations, laws
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn about the three items that require source verification and how to verify each.

tabs.label: shame
tabs.body: For numbers like market size, share, or growth rate, the exact value is important. Look for and compare identical values ​​in tables or official statistics from the original source. In addition to the value, you must check that the base year, unit, and aggregation range are the same.

tabs.label: quote
tabs.body: This includes human statements, papers, and report titles. Make sure that the source actually exists and that the sentences you quote are actually from that source. Even if the title and author are plausible, there are times when they don't exist.

tabs.label: law
tabs.body: Items such as article number, enforcement period, and requirements can have a large impact if they are incorrect. They are compared with official documents from the relevant organizations, and important judgments are reviewed by experts. OpenAI also states in its policy that licensed legal advice requires the involvement of an expert.

tabs.label: Verification Strength
tabs.body: Simple sentence refinement or organizing ideas has a low verification burden. The more information is publicly announced or used in decisions, the more intense the verification becomes. Not everything can be checked with the same intensity, so prioritize checking items that have the highest impact and are difficult to reverse. Priorities are determined by who will be harmed if something is wrong and whether it can be corrected once it is done.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the verification targets, let's take a step-by-step look at the process of comparing claims with the original document.

screens.title: The process of collating the answers into official documents
screens.lead: Let's follow the flow of verifying the AI answer's claim step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

visual.alt: Five-step verification flowchart from claim extraction to original document comparison.
labels: 4 If you don’t know, say you don’t know
5 Follow the document if it is different
If you can't find a supporting sentence, withdraw.
If the value is different from the official document, the document takes precedence.

steps.title: Stage 1 Captain Drawing
steps.body: Pull out the claims you want to verify in your answer: figures, citations, and laws. Rather than trying to check the entire sentence, make a list of only the claims that have the most impact if they are incorrect.

steps.title: Step 2 Find the original document
steps.body: Find the original document on which each claim is based. Claude's document advises that when dealing with long documents, hallucinations are reduced by first extracting the underlying sentences from the document and then working on them.

steps.title: Step 3 Attach Source and Retract
steps.body: Have each claim be accompanied by a citation and source. After receiving the response, the document also introduces a method of asking the person to find a quote to support each claim and, if not found, to withdraw the claim.

steps.title: Step 4: Say you don’t know
steps.body: If you don't know, it's okay to say you don't know. The document explains that this simple method can significantly reduce made-up information. Asking the same question multiple times and comparing the answers to see if they differ from each other is also used to determine doubts.

steps.title: Step 5 Comparison with official documentation
steps.body: If the AI's answer and the value in the official document are different, the document is followed. Again, the key is to compare directly with independent original sources, not AI. Just because you ask the same tool again and get the same answer doesn't mean it's verified.

screens.outro: Now that you have learned the verification flow, let's solve an example of applying it to external presentation materials.

screens.title: Commentary: Applying verification checklist to external presentation materials
screens.lead: The instructor applies validation procedures to AI-drafted external presentation slides. Select the right arrow to see the steps one by one.

steps.title: Check target
steps.body: The target is ten external presentation slides drafted by AI. Since the data is published externally, the intensity of verification must be increased. Once it goes out, it is difficult to get it back, and if it goes wrong, it affects the trust in the organization.

steps.title: Step 1: Cataloging
steps.body: On each slide, make a list of all figures, citations, and legal references. Don't just look at the big, eye-catching numbers, but also collect all the numbers in footnotes and pictures.

steps.title: Step 2: Secure evidence
steps.body: Find the original source for each item. Items for which no evidence is found are deleted or worded weaker. Nothing should be left without attribution.

steps.title: 3-level contrast
steps.body: Verify that the figures have the same values, same base year, and same units as the original text. The quotation verifies that it actually exists and that the sentence is in its source. If the values ​​are different, the original text is followed.

steps.title: Step 4 Human Review
steps.body: The representative reads the entire slide and determines whether it fits the context. Even if the numbers are correct, the context can cause misunderstanding. Legal items are checked by experts. Human review should be a step toward understanding and judging the content, not a formal approval.

steps.title: Step 5 Disclosure Decision
steps.body: Decide whether to disclose the use of AI according to the organization's rules. Disclosure methods and responsible persons follow the rules of the organization and the announcement medium.

screens.outro: Let us address the questions that determine whether this procedure is sufficient.

screens.title: Commentary: Are the verification procedures sufficient?
screens.lead: As you select each question, the instructor's explanation will unfold. After completing the verification process, check yourself with these questions.

items.prompt: Does the confirmation include all figures and citations?
items.answer: If only some are identified, the rest remains at risk. Make sure all items in the list have checkmarks. Delete or weaken the wording of unchecked items.

items.prompt: Are the sources used for verification independent and trustworthy?
items.answer: It is difficult to verify AI answers with each other. It should be checked against evidence independent of the AI, such as original sources or official documents.

items.prompt: Have high-impact items had human review?
items.answer: The more items that are publicly announced or used in decisions, the more human review they require. Legal items are verified by experts.

items.prompt: Has it been determined whether it will be disclosed and who is responsible?
items.answer: It is necessary to decide who did the final verification and how to disclose the fact that AI was used. If you can answer all four of these questions, you can determine that the procedure is sufficient.

screens.outro: Now that I have judged the sufficiency of the procedure, I will summarize the main points of the class.

screens.title: Key point: Facts, figures, and quotations are checked once more by humans.
screens.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class. Read the first question, remembering whether what seems accurate and what is accurate are the same.

paragraphs: There is a difference between what looks accurate and what is accurate. The model can confidently say the wrong answer, so facts, figures and quotes need to be double-checked by humans. The verification targets are figures, citations, and laws, and the most influential items are checked with increasing intensity.

When verifying, it is helpful to have the AI attach a source and then withdraw it if it cannot find evidence. However, the final criterion is original sources and official documents independent of AI. The results that are sent out to the outside world are determined whether they will be made public and who is responsible.

callout.label: standards to remember
callout.text: A confident tone is not evidence. Only write facts that have been compared with the original source.

checks.intro: Put your verification flow in the right order. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Put the flow of verifying the AI answer’s claims in the correct order.
items: Select figures, citations, and legal claims to be confirmed in the answer
Find the original document that serves as the basis
Attach a source to each claim and retract it if you can't find supporting sentences.
If values differ from the official documentation, follow the documentation
checks.explain: First, the verification target is separated, the original document is secured, the source is attached, and finally, it is compared with the official document and if there is a discrepancy, the document is followed.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: We checked the numbers in the report written by the AI by asking another AI to see if they were correct. What is the biggest limitation of this procedure?
options: The second AI can't read numbers at all
Verification takes always longer than human review
Not verified by independent, reliable sources
Statutory items cannot be verified by any means.
checks.explain: It is difficult to verify AI answers with each other. It should be checked against independent evidence, such as original sources or official documents.

wrong.0: The question is not whether it is readable, but whether the basis used for verification is independent.
wrong.1: The limitation is not time, but reliability of evidence.
wrong.3: Legislation can be verified by comparing it with the official documents of the competent authorities and reviewing them by experts.

glossary.def: This is a phenomenon in which a model makes something that is not true seem plausible.
These are items that can have a big impact if they are wrong, such as figures, citations, or laws.
The task is to find the original source of the claim and compare whether it is the same.
This is the stage where the person in charge reads the results and determines the context and impact.
It is about disclosing the fact that AI was used according to the rules of the organization and media.

misconceptions.myth: If AI speaks confidently, it is correct.
misconceptions.fact: The model can speak confidently even if the answer is wrong. Confident speech and accuracy are different, so you need to check the evidence separately.

misconceptions.myth: If there is a search function, verification is not necessary.
misconceptions.fact: Tools like search, data analytics, and deep research increase accuracy but do not eliminate errors. Check the source for important information by opening the link directly.

misconceptions.myth: If you ask the AI again and get the same answer, it has been verified.
misconceptions.fact: The same tool can repeat the same error. If you ask the same question multiple times and the answers are discrepant, it can be a clue to doubt, but because it is the same, it does not guarantee that it is correct, so it is necessary to check with independent original sources.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Facts, figures and quotes are double-checked by humans.
For items with greater impact, increase the intensity of verification.
Please attach the source and retract if there is no basis.
The basis for verification is original sources and official documents independent of AI.
